title: Networking and offline
summary: fetch on mobile, timeouts and retries, detecting connectivity, and queueing writes so the app keeps working offline.

sections.title: fetch works, with caveats
sections.body:
React Native provides `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest` and `WebSocket`. Mobile networks are slow and flaky, so:

- Always set a timeout with an `AbortController`; a request on a dead connection may hang for a long time.
- Retry idempotent requests (GET, PUT with the same body) with exponential backoff and jitter; do not blindly retry non-idempotent POSTs.
- iOS blocks plain `http://` by default (App Transport Security) and Android blocks cleartext traffic by default from API 28.

sections.title: Connectivity
sections.body: A network info module reports whether the device is connected and whether the internet is reachable. Being on Wi-Fi does not mean requests will succeed, so treat it as a hint and still handle failures. Refetch stale data when the app returns to the foreground or the connection comes back.

sections.title: An offline queue
sections.body:
An offline-first app writes locally first and syncs later. User actions go into a persisted queue of mutations. When online, the queue sends them **in order**, one at a time, removing each only after the server confirms it. A failure leaves the item at the head and stops the flush so ordering holds; retries back off. Give each mutation a client-generated id so the server can ignore a duplicate if a response was lost and the app retries.

Exercises here run as TypeScript in a browser sandbox with no React Native runtime, so they model this logic as plain functions and reducers. The same functions drop straight into a real app: call them from a component, a hook or a store. The exercise models the queue with an injected `send` function and an `online` flag.

sections.title: Optimistic updates
sections.body: Show the change immediately, send it in the background, and roll back with a message if it fails. Keep the previous value so the rollback is exact.

pitfalls: No timeout, so a request on a dead network hangs.
Retrying POSTs without an idempotency key, creating duplicates.
Removing a queued mutation before the server confirms it.
Trusting the connectivity flag instead of handling request failures.

gotchas.question: Why should an offline queue stop at the first failure instead of skipping it?
gotchas.answer: Later mutations may depend on earlier ones (create then edit). Sending them out of order can fail or corrupt data, so keep order and retry the head.

gotchas.question: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
gotchas.answer: Without it, many clients that failed together retry together and overload the server again. Random jitter spreads the retries out.

gotchas.question: Does `fetch` reject on a 500 response?
gotchas.answer: No. `fetch` only rejects on network failure or abort. Check `response.ok` or `status` yourself.
